about: Why a settlement is where it is, and what follows from that: a crossing has an inn because travellers are why it exists, a fishing hamlet has none; a monastery lodges strangers in its guest-hall and a fort in its canteen; a hamlet's shrine is a stone by the track and its goods are sold from a door. Each founding names the settlement's heart (where the company stands in it), says once why the place is there (in the company's notes, not in the scene), describes the heart by day as it is seen, heard and smelled (doc/authoring/narratology.md), says what is seen of the place from the road, gives what goes on there, may add one place of its own, and prefers the work its people do. {name} is the settlement, {river} the river it is by, {water} the lake or the sea, {pass} the pass, {cult} its god, {keeper} the one who keeps the house where travellers sleep, {trade} what it lives by.

inn.night: {name} is shuttered for the night. A lamp burns over the door of {inn}.

alehouse.night: {name} is dark for the night, all but {keeper}'s window, where voices still carry.
scene: {keeper}'s alehouse is a front room with a barrel on trestles by the hearth and two benches worn smooth. It smells of peat smoke and sour malt, and the ale is drawn into horn cups.
{keeper}'s alehouse is a kitchen that people drink in, hot from the range, with hams hung in the smoke above it. A cat sleeps on the warm end of the settle.
Under a low roof the brewing is done in the back and the drinking in the front. The room smells of wort and woodsmoke.

guesthouse.night: The brothers' gate is shut, but a lamp burns over it, and a bell hangs by it for late comers.
scene: The guest-hall is long and whitewashed, with a row of cots down one wall and a fire at the far end, kept in all night. It smells of lye soap and tallow.

Plain benches stand round a scrubbed table and a fire of small logs. On the whitewash above the hearth the rule of the house is written out in a careful hand, and its first line says that no one is turned away.

canteen.night: Torches burn along the wall of {name}, and a sentry walks its length and back.
scene: The canteen is a lean-to against the inside of the wall, with a counter, two barrels and a slate of chalked debts. It smells of leather, smoke and spilled beer.
Off-duty soldiers sit along the canteen's benches with their boots off and their belts hung on the pegs above them. Dice rattle in a cup, and the beer is thin and cold.

none.night: {name} is dark, and smells of cold hearths. A dog barks once, then is quiet.

tower.name: the tower of the shrine
tower.unseen: A stair goes up inside the tower wall, worn hollow in the middle of every step, to where the bell hangs.
tower.seen: From the top of the tower {name} lies below you, its roofs and its yards, and the country round it as far as the light goes.
tower.change: Climb the tower and look out over {name}

chapel.room: the chapel of the brothers' house

garrison.door: the chapel door in the wall

crossing.sight: the river shining and the crossing over it
why: {name} is here because the road has to cross the {river}, and here it can. The crossing came first, and the houses after.
{name} is where the {river} runs shallow enough to wade, and nowhere else does for a day's walk: the road came to it for that, and the houses after.
scene: The road runs down between the houses of {name} and straight into the {river}, and comes out on the far bank dark with wet. The water is loud over the stones, and the bank smells of mud and trodden weed.
At {name} the houses stand close along the bank where the road goes down into the {river}. A rope is strung across the water on posts, green where hands have held it.

{name} is a crossing with houses at each end of it, the near end the larger, and the {river} between them, brown and quick. On this side the mud is churned by hooves and cartwheels down to the water's edge.
life: A carter stands thigh-deep in the water with his breeches rolled, hauling at the bridle of a horse that will not come.
A woman on the far bank is calling for the ferry over the noise of the ford.
Two drovers stand at the edge with sticks in the water, arguing whether it has risen since yesterday.

place.name: the crossing stones
place.scene: Flat stones step across the {river}, slick and green below the waterline. Spray wets the shins of anyone crossing.

things.name: the notched post
things.seen: The notched post leans a little downstream.
things.closer: Each notch has a year cut beside it. The highest is older than anyone in {name}, and it is above your head.

why: Boats put in at {name} because the {water} is shallow and foul everywhere else along this shore, and what boats bring in, carts take away.
{name} is the one place on this shore where a boat can lie safe in a blow, and so everything that comes over the {water} comes in here.
scene: Boats lie drawn up keel to keel on the shingle at {name}, and the houses come right down to them, nets hung on every fence. The air is salt and tar, and the shingle rattles back with every wave.

A quay of grey stone runs out into the water at {name}, its edge worn round and green with weed, and the town climbs behind it. Gulls sit along it in a row, facing the wind, over the slap of water on stone.
life: A boat is coming in under half its sail, and a man waits on the quay with a coil of rope over his arm.
A boatwright is tarring an upturned hull on trestles, and the smell hangs over the shingle.
A woman sells mackerel straight off a boat, holding each up by the tail and calling its price.

place.name: the boat-sheds
place.scene: Long low sheds stand open to the water, with boats inside in every stage of being built or mended: ribs like a whale's, an oar with a split blade. Shavings and tar lie thick underfoot, and an adze knocks at the back.

things.name: the hull half planked
things.seen: A hull stands half planked in the nearest shed, its ribs bare at the stern.
things.closer: A name is chalked on the stem, rubbed out, and chalked again: her builder has not settled what to call her.

why: {name} is here for the fish that come in along this shore, and has lived off them since its first boat.
{name} lives off the water: its houses were built with their backs to the land.
scene: Split fish hang drying on racks along the water at {name}, silver going to brown. The houses stand back behind the racks, low and grey.
{name} is a handful of low houses and a great many nets, hung dripping from poles along the shore. Gulls wheel and scream over the drying-ground.
Boats lie bottom-up on the bank at {name}. The paths between the houses are paved with crushed shells that crunch underfoot.
life: Two women are gutting fish into a bucket and talking low.
Gulls stand along a ridge-pole, watching the gutting-bench.
A boy is mending a net across his knees, the twine wet in his fingers.

workings.sight: the workings scarred into the ground beyond
why: {name} is where the {trade} is; nothing else would have brought people here.
The {trade} at {name} was found in the grandmothers' time, and the place has been digging ever since.

tin: The smelting-hearths at {name} smoke day and night, and grey slag lies in heaps along the stream. The air tastes of metal.
Spoil-heaps stand round {name} like a second set of hills, grey and bare, and the houses are built of the same grey stone. Under the ground a pump thuds, slow and regular.
The pit-head at {name} is a yard of trodden mud round a winding-wheel, with ore stacked in heaps. The wheel creaks as it turns, and cold air breathes up out of the shaft.
slate: Half a hillside has been cut away above {name} in steps, and the houses are roofed and walled and floored with what came out of it. The tap of the splitters' mallets comes down off the steps.
The quarry-yard at {name} is slate in stacks and in splinters, some split so thin the light shows through. Blue-grey dust lies on everything.
salt: Steam stands over the salt-pans at {name} on the stillest day, and the ground round them is white and crunches underfoot. The air stings the eyes.
The salt-pans at {name} are shallow, square and steaming, with a fire and a raker at each. The air tastes of the sea.
peat: The peat-banks at {name} are cut back from the houses in long black steps, and the stacks drying beside them are taller than the houses. The ground gives underfoot.
Peat smoke hangs over {name}, brown and sweet, from every chimney. The ground is black and soft, and the cuttings shine wet beyond the houses.

life: A string of ponies comes down from the workings with full panniers, heads low, hooves clattering on the stones.
A horn sounds up at the workings for the change of shift.
A man comes up from the workings black with dust, blinking at the daylight.

tin.name: the adit mouth
tin.scene: The mine goes into the hill here, a black square mouth propped with timber. Cold air comes out of it steadily. A lamp burns in a niche beside it, and before the lamp lie a nail, a heel of bread and a button.

iron.name: the bloomery
iron.scene: A low clay hearth like a squat chimney, with bellows at its foot and a heap of red ore and a heap of charcoal beside it. The bloom comes out glowing, a spongy lump the hammermen beat until the slag runs out.

slate.name: the quarry face
slate.scene: The quarry face goes up in steps three times a man's height, blue-grey and wet. Splitters sit at its foot with their mallets, and now and then a slab comes away clean and rings.

salt.name: the boiling-house
salt.scene: Inside the boiling-house the steam is thick. The pans seethe over their fires, and the salt comes off the rakes grey and dries white in baskets.

peat.name: the peat-stacks
peat.scene: The peat is stacked to dry in walls taller than a man, with passages between them. The air between them is still and smells of earth and smoke.

yard.sight: the yard where its work is done
why: {name} lives by {trade}, and grew up round the yard where it is worked.
{name} is here because the {trade} is: the houses came after the work, and fit round it as they can.

charcoal: {name} is a clearing in the wood with the houses round its edge and the clamps smoking under their turf in the middle. The smoke is blue and bitter.
Grey ash films the house-walls at {name}, and the leaves of the trees round the clearing. The clamps smoke under their turf in the middle, and the air is bitter with them.
timber: Trunks lie stacked at {name}, stripped and waiting, and the saw in the sawpit rasps all day. The air is gold with sawdust and smells of resin.
{name} is built and fenced of split timber, and smells of resin. Axes knock in the trees beyond.
reed: Reed stands in ricks at {name} taller than the houses, and every roof is thatched with it, gold on top and grey beneath. The ricks rustle in the wind.
Bundles of reed lean against every wall at {name} to dry, so that the whole place rustles when the wind gets up. It smells of the marsh.
whale oil: The try-works at {name} are a row of great iron pots over fire-pits on the shore, and the whole place reeks of rendered fat. Black smoke rolls off them toward the sea.
Jawbones stand as gateposts at {name}, and the fences are made of ribs. The shingle is greasy underfoot, and gulls scream over the shore.
furs: Pelts hang stretched on frames all round {name}, drying in the wind, and the place is full of the faint sour smell of them.
{name} is a long hall inside a stockade, with frames of stretched pelts on every side. The frames creak in the wind, and the smell of the pelts is faint and sour.
honey: Hives stand in rows along every wall at {name}, and the air hums with bees. People move slowly between them, and keep their hands still.
{name} smells of wax and clover, and the bees hum along every wall.

life: A loaded cart grinds past, its axle squealing, and the dust of its load drifts after it.
Two of the workers sit on a stack at their bread and cheese, passing a jug between them.
A child staggers past with a full basket, red in the face.

why: {name} is fields first and a village second: everyone in it is a farmer when it matters, at sowing and at harvest.
{name} grew up where the land was good and the water near, and has lived by its fields ever since.

place.name: the mill
place.scene: The mill sits over the stream, and the race thunders under the floor. Flour lies on every beam, and the room trembles with the turning of the stones.

things.name: the mill-wheel
things.seen: The wheel turns slowly over the race, dripping.
things.closer: One paddle is new, pale wood among the black, put in this spring.

monastery.sight: the long wall of the brothers' house, and a bell-cote over the gate
why: {name} grew up round the brothers' house of {cult}: the brothers came for the quiet, and the village came after them to farm and to sell.
There were brothers at {name} before there was a {name}: the village is the farms that feed them and the people who sell them things.
scene: A wall runs round the brothers' house at {name}, with the village built against the outside of it. The gate stands open by day, and the bell over it stirs in the wind.

The gate-yard of {name} is swept clean to the cobbles, and smells of wet stone and beeswax from the chapel door. The brothers' house stands at the back of it behind a low wall, and the village crowds round the front.
life: A bell rings in the brothers' house, and two lay brothers in the yard stand still until it stops.
A brother sells small beer and honey at the gate, counting the coins into a wooden bowl.
Inside the brothers' house a voice is practising a chant, the same four notes over and over.

place.name: the cloister
place.scene: A square of grass lies inside a covered walk, with a well in the middle. The walk smells of cold stone and candle-smoke, and water drips far down the well.

things.name: the book left open on the bench
things.seen: A book lies face down and open on the bench in the cloister walk.
things.closer: It is the house's own chronicle, in many hands. The last entry is a week old, and stops in the middle of a word.

fortress.sight: a wall round the top of the rise, and a gate-tower
why: {name} is a fort first. It holds the {pass} for whoever holds it, and the village is what grew up in its shadow to sell the garrison bread and beer.
A wall was built across the {pass} at {name} long ago, and soldiers have been paid to stand on it ever since.
scene: A wall of rough stone goes round the top of the rise at {name}, with a gate-tower that leans a little. Inside it the yard is trodden mud round a well, and the wind hums through the arrow-slits of the long hall.
The bailey of {name} is a muddy yard inside a wall, with the hall on one side and the stables on the other. It smells of horses and woodsmoke, and boots ring on the flags by the well.
life: A sergeant is drilling four soldiers in the mud, his voice flat and hoarse, their spear-butts thudding down together.
A sentry on the wall-walk stands with a hand over her eyes, looking down the empty road.
A soldier sits on an upturned bucket, stitching a boot with waxed thread.

place.name: the gate-tower
place.scene: The gate-tower is cold and smells of smoke and leather. A ladder goes up to the top, where the road can be seen both ways to the edge of the country.

view.name: the ladder to the top of the gate-tower
view.unseen: The ladder's rungs are worn pale in the middle, and the trap at the top stands open.
view.seen: On the roof of the gate-tower the wind is cold, and the country lies open all round, the road running out of it both ways.
view.change: Climb to the top of the gate-tower

ancient.sight: a ring of great old stones in the middle of it
why: {name} is built round the makers' well, which is older than the town: it goes down further than anyone has followed it, and has never once run dry.
Before there was {name} there was the makers' well, and the first settlers drank from it and stayed.
scene: The houses of {name} stand in a ring round a paved place of great old stones, too big and too square for anyone living to have laid them. In the middle the makers' well opens, and cold air comes up out of it.
At {name} the new houses stand on old walls, rough stone laid on dressed, the joins plain to see. The paving where the lanes meet is worn into hollows that hold the rain.
life: A line of people with buckets waits at the old well, and the windlass creaks as each pail comes up.
Children are daring each other to drop a stone down the old well and count; the oldest says she got to twenty.
A ring of plaited straw hangs on the tallest of the old stones.

place.name: the makers' well
place.scene: A shaft of dressed stone, wider than a cart, with steps cut spiralling down the inside of it to the water a long way below. The stone at the lip is worn into grooves by ropes. The air coming up out of it is cold and smells of iron.

below.name: the foot of the makers' well
below.way: the stair down the makers' well
below.scene: The steps go down and round the inside of the shaft, worn hollow in the middle, and the daylight shrinks to a coin overhead. At the bottom the water is black, still and very cold.

things.name: the words cut in the last step
things.seen: Small words are cut into the last step above the water, in the old script, worn but whole.
things.closer: The letters are the makers': deep, square, every one the same height, cut by someone who meant them to last as long as the well.
things.known: The words on the last step of the makers' well at {name}, in the old script: WATER FOR THOSE AFTER US. ASK IT NOTHING ELSE.

why: The folk of {name} came here within living memory, by wagon, and some of the wagons are still in use as houses.
The folk of {name} came from far off; only the children were born here.
scene: {name} is half houses and half wagons with their wheels taken off, painted saffron and rose and a deep blue. Cook-smoke drifts between them, smelling of cumin and charred onion.
The camp at {name} is awnings and cook-fires and washing on every line, the wagons drawn up in a ring. Dogs bark at the edge of the ring.
life: A man is playing a fiddle under an awning, and stops when he sees you looking.
An old woman is telling a story to a ring of children in a tongue you do not have, and they laugh together at the same places.
Two families share one fire, their pots crowded together on the irons, and the smell of both drifts across the camp.

market.sight: the market cross and the roofs of the stalls
why: {name} is where the roads of the country meet, and so where its goods do: whatever is made in the country is bought and sold here at least once.
{name} holds the country's market: whatever the country makes or needs comes through it.
scene: Stalls stand in rows across the market-place of {name}, under awnings faded to the colour of straw. The cobbles are slick with trodden leaves. The air smells of new bread and spilt ale.
A stone market cross stands in the middle of the square at {name}, its steps worn into dips. Shutters bang open along the houses, and carts grind over the cobbles.
life: A baker's boy works through the crowd with a tray of loaves on his head.
A tinker beats a dent out of a pan, and the ringing carries across the square.
A carter backs his horse in between the stalls, swearing at it softly.
